paragraphs.text: Familial adult myoclonic epilepsy, also called benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME or FAME), is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by shivering-like tremors of cortical origin, myoclonus, and epilepsy (Madia et al., 2008). De Fusco et al. (2014) described the disorder, which they called autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME), as a familial disorder with cortical reflex myoclonus. It shows as action-induced shivering movements of the hands and jerking of the upper limbs, variably associated with focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures of variable severity. A minority of patients have borderline or moderately impaired cognition, and myoclonus often worsens in advanced age.

paragraphs.text: Guerrini et al. (2001) described a pedigree in which 8 individuals had a nonprogressive disorder with onset between 12 and 50 years of age. All had mainly distal, semicontinuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 had complex partial seizures. Most rarely had seizures and had normal cognition, but 3 individuals with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. All patients had frontotemporal as well as generalized interictal EEG abnormalities. Neurophysiologic studies showed that the myoclonus was cortical in origin. In 5 patients, EEG over the contralateral rolandic area was coherent with EMG at 8 to 25 Hz, and EEG activity preceded EMG activity by 8 to 15 ms; ipsilateral coherence in 2 patients was consistent with transcallosal spread. Patients had an enhanced C-reflex and high-amplitude somatosensory and visual evoked potentials. Compared with controls, they also had a reduced resting motor threshold to transcranial magnetic stimulation and a shortened post-MEP silent period. The authors suggested that these findings reflect diffuse cortical hyperexcitability.

paragraphs.text: Labauge et al. (2002) described a 4-generation European family with 18 members and familial adult myoclonic epilepsy. Ten living and 3 deceased relatives were affected. In the 10 living patients, mean age at onset was 41 years (range, 30-60 years). Eight of the 13 affected individuals had generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Electrophysiologic studies in 5 patients confirmed the diagnosis of FAME.

paragraphs.text: Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy. Eleven members, aged 24 to 56 years (mean, 39.2 years), had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 of them had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study confirmed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members. Three presymptomatic members had giant somatosensory evoked potential components and an enhanced long loop reflex I; after 1.5 years of follow-up, these members developed hand tremor and myoclonus of the upper limbs.

paragraphs.text: Suppa et al. (2009) described an Italian family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy (FCMTE). Clinically affected family members had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus of the eyelids during blinking. Neuropsychological testing showed visuospatial impairment, which the authors suggested may be due to temporal lobe dysfunction. Neurophysiologic studies suggested increased excitability of the primary motor cortex with normal sensorimotor integration.

paragraphs.text: Crompton et al. (2012) described a 6-generation kindred of European descent, ascertained in New Zealand and Australia, with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy. All 55 affected family members had fine hand tremor, usually beginning in adolescence (median age 15 years; range 4-60 years). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%) and began later than the hand tremor (median age 17 years; range 5-60 years). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range 18-76 years); they were uncommon and occurred around sleep onset after severe generalized myoclonus. Neurophysiologic testing showed features of cortical reflex myoclonus. The authors concluded that the most common phenotype in this family was a mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, together with subtle proximal myoclonus.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) described a 4-generation Tuscan family (family B) with 5 affected members. All had postural myoclonus of the hands and upper limbs, and cortical tremor was the presenting symptom, starting between ages 18 and 50 years. All but one had epilepsy with rare generalized tonic-clonic seizures, at times triggered by visual stimuli; 2 patients also had drug-resistant focal motor or complex partial seizures. One patient had borderline cognitive level and the others had normal intelligence. Jerk-locked back-averaged EEG, somatosensory evoked potentials, and long-loop reflex studies were consistent with cortical reflex myoclonus. Brain MRI was normal where performed.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) summarized the clinical features of 22 FAME families. The families were mainly Italian; others were Australian/New Zealand, Sephardic Jewish (Iraqi and Israeli), South African, French/Spanish, French, and Syrian. Patients had cortical myoclonic tremor and myoclonic and later generalized tonic-clonic seizures, with onset usually in the second to third decade. Expressivity varied within and between families, and the frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures ranged from 15% to 100% across families. Some families also had focal seizures. In a large Australian/New Zealand family of European ancestry (Family 1), all 55 affected members had myoclonus/cortical tremor, 8 (15%) had tonic-clonic seizures, and 2 (4%) had focal seizures; mean age of onset was 18.6 years, with a range of 4 to 60 years.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of 2 Tuscan families with autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy mapped to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2, De Fusco et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous in-frame insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B gene (c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG), resulting in replacement of 5 amino acids (HGGAL) in the third intracellular loop by 4 new residues (QFGR) (p.H225_L229delinsQFGR). The variant was found by candidate gene sequencing, segregated completely with the disease, and was absent from 575 Tuscan controls, dbSNP, the Exome Variant Server, and 1000 Genomes; targeted next-generation sequencing of the critical region in 2 affected members found it to be the only relevant change. The 2 families shared the disease haplotype across the critical region. The mutant receptor localized and internalized normally in HeLa cells, but failed to form a stable complex with spinophilin after epinephrine stimulation in CosM6 cells, and spinophilin did not raise the EC50 for epinephrine-stimulated Ca(2+)-activated Cl- current with the mutant receptor in Xenopus oocytes, suggesting a gain-of-function effect.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of families with FAME2, Corbett et al. (2019) identified an expansion of an ATTTT repeat together with an inserted ATTTC repeat within the first intron of the STARD7 gene. The change was first detected by analysis of whole-genome sequencing data from 3 families (Families 1, 3, and 19) with ExpansionHunter and exSTRa and was absent from WGS data on 69 controls. By repeat-primed PCR, the ATTTC expansion was found in all 137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported FAME2 families, in all 20 affected individuals from 6 additional multiplex families, and in 1 of 52 unrelated singleton cases (158 of 158 typically affected individuals from 22 families); it was not found in 28 controls. Long-read sequencing showed a repeat structure of (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n on the forward strand; in one patient from Family 1, a SMRT read contained 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats and a nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats, which the authors suggested reflected somatic variation, and a patient from Family 5 had 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats (4645 bp in total). STARD7 mRNA and protein levels were not altered in patient fibroblasts.
